text_blocks.snippet: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is typically managed through a combination of lifestyle changes, prescription medications, and—in specific cases—specialized medical procedures.
snippet_highlighted_words: lifestyle changes, prescription medications, and—in specific cases—specialized medical procedures

text_blocks.snippet: Heart-healthy habits form the foundation of treatment and can improve the effectiveness of medications:

list.snippet: Dietary Changes: Follow the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) eating plan, which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on saturated fats.
Sodium Reduction: Lower salt and sodium intake (aiming for less than 2,000 mg per day) to help drop blood pressure.
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise (such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming) and resistance training.
Weight Management: Achieve and maintain a healthy body weight.
Limit Alcohol and Avoid Tobacco: Reduce or stop alcohol consumption and quit smoking.

text_blocks.snippet: When lifestyle changes are not enough, doctors frequently prescribe one or more classes of blood pressure medications. Common first-line drug classes include:

list.snippet: ACE Inhibitors (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors): Relax and widen blood vessels (e.g., lisinopril, ramipril).
ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers): Block the action of chemicals that narrow blood vessels (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers: Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells to allow vessels to relax (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the body flush out excess sodium and water, reducing fluid volume (e.g., thiazides like hydrochlorothiazide).

Other Medications: Depending on individual health needs or coexisting conditions (like heart disease or kidney issues), providers may use beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, or central-acting agents. Many patients require a combination of two or more drugs.

Renal Denervation: A minimally invasive procedure that uses energy pulses to calm overactive nerves near the kidneys for patients whose blood pressure remains uncontrolled despite lifestyle changes and multiple medications.

text_blocks.snippet: You can learn more about daily management strategies on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Guide or review medication classes through the American Heart Association Drug Guide.
